archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose underlying efficiency and point differential belong to a playoff side, held at .500 by giveaways, a quarterback detour and an offense that leans on a run game that doesn't work.

report.headline: An elite defense dragged to .500 by turnovers and a stubborn run game
report.take:
Seattle is still, at heart, last year's team on defense. The 2025 unit led the league in EPA allowed and points allowed on the way to 14 wins, and this one is nearly as suffocating: second in EPA allowed per play, first in yards allowed per game, second in success rate and third-down rate allowed, and first in explosive pass rate allowed. That rests on a pass rush that generates pressure on 30.8% of dropbacks, third in the league, and a back end that erases the deep ball. This is not a defense padding its numbers against bad offenses; it held Kansas City to three points and smothered a top-10 Patriots attack in the opener.

The record says otherwise because of the other side of the ball. The offense ranks 25th in EPA per play, and the split explains why: passing is roughly league average while the run game is 29th in rush EPA, behind a line that allows pressure more often than any other in football and converts short yardage worse than anyone. Despite that, Seattle passes well below expectation, 27th in pass rate over expected. Add the quarterback detour, with Drew Lock starting Weeks 2 through 6, and the giveaways piled up: four turnovers in the home loss to San Francisco, three each at Washington and Denver. The bulk of the 14 turnovers came in that stretch, and all three losses in it were by three points or fewer.

What the numbers hide is that this is a positive-differential team that has been slightly unlucky rather than lucky. Seattle is +26 on the season, the differential implies 4.5 wins, and the turnover margin per game ranks 27th, the kind of number that tends to drift back toward neutral. Special teams, third in EPA per game, and a coach who goes for it on every fourth down he can add hidden value. The one real defensive leak is the red zone, where opponents score touchdowns 78.6% of the time, 29th, which is why points allowed trail yardage allowed.

The worry is last week. Chicago put 34 on this defense with 247 passing yards and 126 rushing, and Seattle played without Uchenna Nwosu and lost Leonard Williams to a stinger in-game. If that was a one-off, Darnold's return and a softer stretch of schedule point toward a winning finish and a wild-card push; San Francisco at 6-1 looks out of reach for the division unless the head-to-head in Week 12 flips it.

strengths.title: A top-three defense on every axis
strengths.body: Seattle ranks second in EPA allowed per play and success rate allowed and first in yards allowed per game, with no weakness in pass or run EPA allowed. It carries over from a 2025 unit that led the league, so this is a scheme and roster, not a hot start. It should hold, provided the front gets healthy.

strengths.title: Pressure without sacrificing the deep ball
strengths.body: The rush gets home on 30.8% of dropbacks and hits the quarterback at the third-highest rate, while the coverage behind it allows the fewest explosive passes in the league. Pressure forcing quick throws plus disciplined depth is why opponents can't create chunk plays. Of all of it, this is the most repeatable.

strengths.title: Hidden yardage from special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add 4.01 EPA a game, third in the league, and the staff goes for it on every eligible fourth down. Those edges help a field-position team with a sputtering offense and tend to persist with the same coaching.

concerns.title: Turnovers have erased the defense's work
concerns.body: The turnover margin per game ranks 27th, and four-, three- and three-giveaway games all ended in close losses. Most of those came during Lock's run, so Darnold's return should help, and the giveaway rate is the stat most likely to regress toward average. Still, an offense that can't run is forced into risky passing downs.

concerns.title: Worst protection in the league, ineffective run
concerns.body: The line allows pressure on 28.1% of dropbacks, last in the league, ranks 29th in run EPA and last in short-yardage conversion. Long time to throw makes the protection look worse, but this is a real flaw, and with Charles Cross listed out it may get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: Running too much, leaking in the red zone
concerns.body: Passing is roughly league average in EPA while rushing is 29th, yet Seattle passes well below expectation. On defense, opponents who reach the red zone score touchdowns at the fourth-worst rate. Both are fixable choices and small-sample swings rather than talent problems, but they have cost close games.

trend.note: Wins and losses have alternated around the quarterback switch: a strong start, a turnover-plagued middle under Lock, a dominant win over Kansas City on Darnold's return, then a lopsided home loss to Chicago.

nextGame.headline: Darnold should finally air it out against a leaky secondary
nextGame.body:
Seattle hosts Arizona as an 11.5-point favorite, a rematch of a 31-7 road win in Week 2. The matchup is lopsided in a specific way: Arizona's run defense is solid, ninth in rush EPA allowed, but its pass defense is 31st in EPA allowed and 30th in explosive pass rate allowed, and opposing WR1s and WR2s have feasted. Its pass rush is also below average, which is the best possible news for the league's leakiest protection. On the other side, Jacoby Brissett gets the ball out quickly, which blunts Seattle's rush somewhat, but the Cardinals rank 26th in points per game and 32nd in points allowed.

Availability tilts further Seattle's way, with caveats. Charles Cross, the left tackle who played 98% of snaps, plus Nwosu and Rashid Shaheed are listed out with return estimates of game day, so their status is genuinely uncertain, and Leonard Williams is questionable after a stinger. Arizona is in worse shape: Kendrick Bourne is done for the year, Michael Wilson is questionable with two broken ribs, both running backs Jeremiyah Love and Bam Knight are questionable, and guard Jon Gaines and defensive tackle Walter Nolen are out.

waysToWin.title: Throw early through Smith-Njigba
waysToWin.body: Arizona has allowed 0.67 EPA per target to WR1s, 30th, and its pass defense ranks 31st overall. Jaxon Smith-Njigba commands far more targets than anyone on the roster, so tilting the plan toward early-down passing plays to Seattle's real edge and away from Arizona's sturdy run defense.

waysToWin.title: Defense smothers a depleted Arizona attack
waysToWin.body: With Bourne gone, Wilson playing hurt at best and both backs questionable, Brissett may have few reliable options against a top-two defense. Seattle held this offense to 95 passing yards and 70 rushing in Week 2.

waysToWin.title: Protection finally holds up
waysToWin.body: Arizona generates pressure at only a 21.2% rate, 24th, so this is the week Seattle's line can give Darnold clean pockets even if Cross sits. Clean pockets plus Arizona's 24th-ranked deep defense opens the shot plays.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways hand Arizona short fields
waysToLose.body: Seattle's close losses were all multi-turnover games, and a 27th-ranked turnover margin is the one thing that keeps an inferior opponent in reach. Arizona's offense can't move the ball consistently on its own, so it needs gifts.

waysToLose.title: Running into Arizona's strength
waysToLose.body: If Seattle sticks with its run-heavy lean, it plays into a top-10 rush defense with a run game ranked 29th in EPA. Stalled drives leave field goals instead of touchdowns and keep the score close.

waysToLose.title: Chicago game was a real crack
waysToLose.body: The defense gave up 34 points and 126 rushing yards last week, with Nwosu out and Williams hurt. If those absences linger and the red-zone leak continues, Arizona's short passing game can steal points.

nextGame.watch: Seattle's early-down pass rate: if Darnold is throwing on first down into Arizona's 31st-ranked pass defense, this is a rout; if it's handoffs into a top-10 run defense, it stays uncomfortably close.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the sustainable piece: it carries over from a league-best 2025 and it is built on pressure and deep coverage rather than takeaways. The turnover margin should improve with Darnold back, and Seattle's slightly negative wins over expected implies the record will catch up to its play. What won't fix itself is the line: last in pressure allowed and short-yardage conversion, with the starting left tackle hurt, it caps the offense near the middle of the league unless the staff tilts toward the passing game that has actually worked.

The schedule is manageable outside the division: Arizona, Dallas, Philadelphia and Carolina are losing teams, and Dallas brings the league's worst defense. The swing games are at San Francisco and the two Rams meetings against a fourth-ranked defense. A 6-3 or 7-2 finish is the realistic center, enough for a wild-card spot; the division likely requires winning in Santa Clara.
swingFactors: Charles Cross's return to the line

confidence.note: Eight games split across two quarterbacks; defense has multi-year backing, offense does not.
